rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to capture all 6 compounds without truncation and map the elution window across nearly the full solvent range. The moderate 20 min slope should give enough spacing to reveal where the critical pairs sit while keeping the run informative.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to cut t_last below 10 min while keeping peaks inside the gradient. The first and last peaks correspond to roughly phi_e ≈ 0.18 and 0.68 in the scout, so a narrower window with a shorter gradient and higher temperature should compress the run efficiently while still covering the observed elution range.

We already have the maximum CRF, so this run exploits the margin by pushing faster conditions: slightly narrower window, shorter gradient, and higher temperature. The goal is to find the speed limit before any pair drops below 1.5 or the last peak moves out of the covered gradient window.

The current method still has comfortable resolution margin, with the limiting pair at R=2.00, so we can press further toward the shortest viable method. This step tests a more aggressive shortening and narrowing at the highest temperature to see whether all pairs remain above 1.5 while reducing total run time further.

The failure at 4 min is the early pair (1,2), so the next best lever is to lower the initial gradient steepness without lengthening the run by widening the upper end of the window. This keeps the method very fast while testing whether a slightly shallower slope restores the first-pair resolution above 1.5.

The limiting pair is the first one, so reducing early retention likely hurts; raising phi0 should test whether that pair is controlled mainly by very low-phi selectivity versus overall slope. Keeping tG at 6 min preserves near-optimal speed while probing whether the window can be shifted upward without losing full resolution.

Raising phi0 worsened the first critical pair, so the next test is the opposite: lower phi0 to give the earliest pair more low-organic separation while keeping the fast 6 min gradient and 60 C. This should reveal whether the speed limit is set mainly by insufficient early retention, and may recover full resolution at a shorter run than the current best methods.

At 0.05–0.65, 6 min, 60 C the limiting pair is right at the threshold, so narrowing the upper end by one step should slightly shallow the gradient and may give a bit more margin for the early pair while keeping the run essentially as fast. This checks whether phi1 can be reduced without sacrificing the late peak window.

The 6 min, 60 C runs show a tradeoff: lowering phi1 helps the first pair but starts to hurt the 4,5 pair, while 0.65 leaves 1,2 right on the edge. Increasing phi1 to 0.70 at the same tG tests whether the later critical pair gains enough without collapsing 1,2 too far, mapping the selectivity balance around the fast 6 min method.

The 6 min, 60 C method at 0.05–0.65 is essentially on the resolution limit, so the cleanest way to recover margin is a slightly shallower gradient at the same temperature and solvent window. This should confirm whether 8 min at 60 C gives full resolution with shorter total analysis time than the current best 8 min, 50 C method.

The data suggest temperature is strongly affecting selectivity: 6 min at 55 C works fully, while 6 min at 60 C pushes the critical pairs to the edge or below. Testing 6 min, 0.10–0.65 at 50 C should show whether lower temperature restores a wider resolution margin while keeping the run faster than the original 8 min, 50 C optimum.

At 50 C and 0.10–0.65, the 6 min run has ample resolution margin, so the next move is to shorten tG to 4 min at the same selectivity conditions. This directly tests whether we can keep all pairs above 1.5 while gaining a substantially faster fully resolved method.

The 4 min, 50 C method still has useful margin, especially on the late critical pair, so trimming phi1 by one step may further focus the gradient on the elution window without lengthening the run. This tests whether we can keep full resolution while using an even tighter and potentially more efficient window.

The 4 min, 50 C runs at phi1 = 0.60 and 0.65 are both fully resolved, with the faster result at phi1 = 0.65; moving to 0.70 should further shorten the late peak. This maps whether the first pair still stays above 1.5 at the most aggressive upper-end window likely to improve total speed.

The current fastest fully resolved method is 0.10–0.70 over 4 min at 50 C, with the first pair still above threshold at R = 1.66. Increasing phi1 one step should further reduce the late retention and test whether that remaining resolution margin is enough to support an even faster optimal method.

At 0.10–0.75 over 4 min and 50 C, the limiting pair is still just safely above threshold, so one more increase in phi1 is the logical speed test. This should show whether the method can be pushed even shorter before the first pair finally falls below R = 1.5.

We have identified 0.10–0.75 at 4 min, 50 C as the fastest fully resolved condition so far, and the remaining question is whether tG can be cut further. A direct 2 min test establishes whether the ultimate speed limit is set by gradient time itself or already by solvent window, with the first pair expected to be decisive.

The 2 min gradient was too steep because the first pair collapsed, so the next lever is to strengthen early retention while keeping the fastest successful 4 min format and high phi1. Lowering phi0 to 0.05 should preferentially help the earliest critical pair and may yield a fully resolved method at least as fast as the current best.

The fastest fully resolved method so far is 0.10–0.75 over 4 min at 50 C, with the first pair only modestly above threshold; dropping temperature one step should increase selectivity margin for that pair. This checks whether a slightly cooler method preserves very short run time while giving a more robust fully resolved optimum.

At 45 C the first pair regains strong margin at 0.10–0.75, so increasing phi1 to 0.80 is the natural next step to see if that extra selectivity headroom can be traded for an even faster fully resolved method. This directly tests whether the 50 C failure at phi1 = 0.80 can be rescued by the cooler temperature.

The 0.10–0.80, 4 min, 45 C method is fully resolved with clear margin on the first pair, so one more increase in phi1 is the best chance to reduce t_last further while still staying above R = 1.5. This is now a boundary search for the shortest still-perfect method.

The 4 min, 45 C series remains fully resolved up to phi1 = 0.85, with the first pair still above threshold, so phi1 = 0.90 is the next step in bracketing the shortest all-resolved method. This should further reduce t_last and reveal whether the first pair finally becomes limiting at this upper-end strength.

Phi1 = 0.90 at 4 min and 45 C is still fully resolved with the first pair right above threshold, so phi1 = 0.95 is the final logical step to locate the edge of full resolution. If it holds, this becomes the shortest perfect method yet; if not, phi1 = 0.90 is confirmed as the optimum boundary.

We have bracketed the best 4 min window, with 0.10–0.90 at 45 C the fastest fully resolved condition so far; the remaining unknown is whether the cooler temperature can support a 2 min gradient. This run tests the only plausible path to a shorter perfect method, and if it fails the 4 min, 0.10–0.90, 45 C condition is effectively confirmed as optimal.

With 2 min gradients ruled out and 0.10–0.90 at 4 min, 45 C already fully resolved but close on the first pair, the last useful check is whether lowering phi0 adds early-pair margin without sacrificing overall speed too much. This probes the final untested degree of freedom around the apparent optimum boundary.
